strengths: The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
The experiments in Table 1 show the efficacy of the method on the given dataset.
Fast-SQN solves the computational efficiency issue by cleverly adding a spline interpolation layer.
The proposed methods are well-motivated and explained well. It covers existing methods as special cases and can be computed efficiently with the proposed FAST-SQN version.
The authors provide a reasonable literature review and the graphs are very elegant.
Feature preprocessing is an important task, as even deep learning methods such as TabPFN require preprocessing to deal with highly-skewed features.
Using PCHIP splines to achieve linear scalability while maintaining smoothness and monotonicity is an interesting proposal.
weaknesses: Table 1 shows better performance of the proposed method but lacks the error bounds, it might be helpful to see the fluctuation if different random seeds are employed for the same model.

Authors cited that Gaussianisation techniques can mean losing intrinsic patterns in the data and are non-differentiable. However, I would argue that methods like Normalising Flows are differentiable, and a few such layers in the beginning might help with this. It would be interesting to see if NF-transformed data lags in performance compared to the methods reported in Table 1.
Only one dataset is discussed, it is hard to say if the results might hold for any kind of data.
Can this transformation also help with Image data? or use of KDE limits applicability to high dimensionality?
Can using these transformation layers with methods that aim at transforming the distribution to standard normal can we reduce the computational complexity of those methods?
Only one real data experiment is provided.

It is hard to tell if the performance improvements are significant, e.g. in table 1, model 3, Fast-SQN only improves RMSE by 0.001 over YJN, mean and standard deviation over multiple runs should be reported.

The proposed method should be a general scaling method for any feature, but it seems only the target feature is normalized in the experiments (line 390 in the paper). I thought rescale input features would be more useful in model training.
One advantage that is emphasized for the proposed method is its differentiability, but if it is only used in the experiment setting in the paper, differentiability doesn't seem to have any advantage.
There are no real justification of support of the method whatsoever.

There is no theoretical support (there is a proposition in the appendix, which is formulated non-rigorously. What type of convergence is this? The KDE is a function of a random quantity, the empirical (random) measure associated with some one-dimensional law, then should I interpret this as ω-wise convergence? Therefore, this is no theoretical contribution).

The numerics are not convincing, only a toy dataset (the California Housing Market) dataset is considered, which is something on sees in introductory text books. Thus, there is also no experimental support for the proposed method.
The convergence in the proposition in the appendix is in the point-open topology, but this is not mentioned, making the statement difficult to interpret.

The experimental section is quite weak, only evaluating on the California housing dataset. The results would be much more convincing if the authors showed benefits on a benchmark of tabular datasets. And, while the authors claim that differentiability is valuable, but don't show that this provides any empirical benefits.

The authors evaluate their method in combination with feedforward neural networks, which are not even close to SotA for tabular data. The choice of model obscures the true potential of the proposed preprocessing method. It's difficult to ascertain whether performance gains are due to the preprocessing itself or the specific architecture of the neural network.

The originality of the proposal and the completeness of the related work section are seriously affected by the fact that the overall proposed approach is the same as KDIT (The Kernel Density Integral Transformation, McCarter, TMLR 2023). In both cases, one uses the KDE to smooth the pdf of a feature, then applies the inverse cdf of a reference distribution.
